::: {.letter-metadata}
**Date:** April 27 [1892].[^1]  
**From:** Elderfield  
**Manuscript:** MS location unknown.  Printed in Coleridge, <i>[Life](other_books/otherbook_40.qmd)</i> 336
:::

My dear [Helen](people/person_1613.qmd)
Thank you for the £8, which I found safely on coming home from hearing the first day of the diocesan conference.  

Poor old Graf, it is not every dog who is buried by the [parish clerk](people/person_2111.qmd), with me walking in solemn procession of one all down the walk behind.  I am glad you were spared the catastrophe, and that [mamma](people/person_1604.qmd) has Koko to divert her mind.  I am afraid [Mr. Brock](people/person_201.qmd) will go to Guernsey, so there is no end of the changes.

The [Miss Jacob](people/person_749.qmd)s are going to have [Miss Finlaison](people/person_512.qmd)'s house for the summer holidays, which will be pleasant for me.  That [Mr. Eames](people/person_465.qmd) who has bought Silkstead is beginning to build a house on the Winchester road, and has put in a keeper at Silkstead who warns people off the white violets on the bank at Green Undys.[^2]

It must have been very delightful seeing [Mr. Beck](people/person_132.qmd)'s hoards and hearing their history, - as good as a museum.  My berberis has just become beautiful, but it is very cold to-day.

Your affectionate aunt
C. M. Yonge

---

[^1]: Dated from the reference to the departure of the Rev. Henry Brock in 1892.
[^2]: Edward Eames (b. 1849/50), auctioneer and surveyor,  bought Silkstead Priors in Compton parish and was living there at the time of the 1901 census.
